title: Declarative GPU feature flagging and IaC guardrails
author: Aisha Patel
summary: A prescriptive pattern for managing GPU-related feature flags (scheduling toggles, kernel rollout, quantization profiles) as first-class Terraform artifacts with policy checks, CI gates, and runtime wiring. This doc defines modules, policies, rollout steps, and monitoring contracts to safely enable/disable inference features across hosted, dedicated, and private environments.
intro: Purpose: reduce blast radius and operational toil when changing GPU runtime behavior by: (1) codifying flags in Terraform, (2) enforcing policy-as-code at merge time, (3) providing a repeatable canary + automated rollback flow, and (4) instrumenting observability for safety and cost impact.
motivation: GPU runtime changes (e.g., new kernels, mixed-precision switches, KV cache prefetch tweaks) frequently affect latency, cost, and correctness. Ad hoc toggles in code or ad hoc scripts lead to drift, lack of audit, and slow incident response. Treating flags as IaC gives us versioning, reviewability, and a single source of truth that the deployment control plane and SREs can rely on.
goals:
- Make GPU-related feature flags discoverable and auditable
- Prevent unsafe flag combinations via pre-merge policy checks
- Provide a low-friction canary rollout path with automated monitoring
- Ensure rollbacks are fast, measured, and reversible
- Keep runtime flag evaluation light-weight and decoupled from control plane
non_goals:
- This doc does not replace application-level feature flags (end-user UI toggles)
- Not a detailed kernel implementation guide — focus is operational control, not kernel dev
scope: Applies to flags that change inference serving behavior or allocation semantics: kernel selection, mixed-precision enablement, prefix/KV caching modes, tenant preemption preferences, and autoscaling aggressiveness. Excludes per-request prompt-level flags and user-visible product feature flags.
design_overview: High level: 1) Flags are defined in a central Terraform module (gpu_flag). 2) Each environment (prod/dedicated/staging/private) consumes the module and sets values in environment-specific tfvars tracked in Git. 3) A GitHub Actions pipeline runs policy-as-code (OPA checks) + integration canaries (lightweight smoke tests) on PRs. 4) Runtime path: serving control plane reads the consolidated flag state from an immutable configuration store (S3/GCS) generated by terraform apply and served by a read-optimized metadata service. 5) Telemetry tags on inference traces annotate which flags were active.
policy_and_checks:
Pre-merge checks (run in CI):
- OPA/rego rules ensure: no conflicting flags enabled simultaneously (e.g., kernel_x_v2 + kernel_x_safe_mode), rollout_percent in [0,100], owner is non-empty, and any flag that reduces isolation requires an approved exception.
- tfsec/static analysis verifies there are no secrets in tfvars.
- Integration smoke: a lightweight canary job runs the serving smoke harness against a staging namespace with the new flags applied.

Example Rego rule (human readable):
- Deny if rollout_percent > 0 and enabled == false (misconfigured semantics).
- Deny if name contains "private_" and target environment != private.
canary_and_rollout_procedure:
1) Create feature-flag TF change in a branch targeting the appropriate env overlay (e.g., env/prod). 2) Open PR with 'flag: <name>' label. 3) CI runs OPA checks + staging smoke tests. 4) Once CI passes, merge to main. 5) Terraform apply runs in GitOps runner and writes a new flags manifest to stable bucket (s3://redwood-config/flags/<env>/<timestamp>.json). 6) Router reads manifest and begins rollout by evaluating 'rollout_percent' (deterministic hashing on tenant id) and activating the flag for the first X% of tenants. 7) Observe for 1h: latency P95, error rate, cost per request, and qualitative QA checks. 8) If metrics breach thresholds (see guardrail thresholds), automatically trigger rollback-conductor to revert the tf change or set rollout_percent back to previous value.

Guardrail thresholds (example):
- latency_p95 increase > 18% over baseline -> alert
- request_error_rate increase > 1.0 percentage point -> alert
- cost_per_token increase > 12% -> alert

Automated rollback policy: the monitoring job can open a hotfix PR that sets the flag back to the previous stable tag and auto-merge under an emergency policy if SRE approves.
ci_cd_integration:
- GitHub Actions pipeline jobs: validate, opa_check, smoke_canary, plan, apply (apply runs only in main branch via runner with least-privilege service account).
- Example job fragment:

```yaml
jobs:
  opa_check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - run: opa test ./policy -v
  smoke_canary:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./ci/smoke_canary.sh --env=staging --flag-manifest=./out/flags.json
```

- Secrets and cloud creds: restrict terraform apply runner to dedicated CI machine with ephemeral creds and narrow IAM role: flags:Write to config-bucket, read-only on infra-state, no admin on compute resources.
runtime_wiring:
- The serving control plane uses a read-only manifest derived from Terraform outputs. Manifests are versioned and immutable (content-addressed).
- Runtime evaluation code is simple: lookup flag_name -> {enabled, rollout_percent, metadata}. Hash tenant_id % 100 < rollout_percent -> enabled for tenant.
- Flag evaluation must be non-blocking and default to safe state (disabled) if manifest is unreachable.
- Telemetry: attach flag_version and active_flag_list as tags to traces and span logs to enable post-hoc rollback/traffic-slicing analysis.
monitoring_and_alerting:
Required metrics and dashboards:
- Flag rollout dashboard: flag name, version, rollout_percent, active_tenants_count, applied_regions
- Safety signals: latency_p50/p95/p99 by flag_version, error_rate by flag_version, cost_per_token by flag_version
- Canary healthcheck SLO: smoke_canary must succeed at > 99% per 5m window during rollout

Alerting playbook:
- SEV1 if latency_p95 increase > 30% and > 5% tenants affected -> paging SRE and Serving Runtime owner
- SEV2 for cost regressions > 25% -> notify FinOps and runtime owner
- All alerts should include: flag name, manifest version, tf commit hash, link to PR and runbook.

migration_and_backfill_plan: For existing ad-hoc flags: 1) Inventory -- run a 2-week discovery job scanning repos and runtime manifests. 2) Create mapping PRs that produce equivalent Terraform gpu_flag resources with rollout_percent set to 0. 3) Run smoke tests and increment rollout_percent in small steps. 4) Deprecate inline toggles and add a blocking pre-merge OPA rule that denies direct changes to runtime flag endpoints without corresponding tf change.\n\nBackfill schedule example: Week 1: inventory and mapping, Week 2: create tf modules and PRs (rollout_percent=0), Week 3-6: staged rollouts and deprecation of old toggles.
runbook_snippets: Quick rollback steps: 1) If a severe regression is detected, run: `terraform -chdir=env/prod plan -var 'kv_cache_prefetch_v2.rollout_percent=0' && terraform -chdir=env/prod apply -auto-approve` (GitOps runner will prefer hotfix PR flow). 2) If apply is blocked, run the emergency API: `curl -X POST https://ops-api.internal/flags/<flag>/override -d '{"enabled":false}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'` (requires on-call SRE token). 3) After rollback, create a postmortem and tag the PR with 'incident:flag-rollout'.
security_and_compliance: - All flag changes must be auditable via Git history and bucket manifest versions. - Sensitive flags (those that affect tenant isolation or data residency) must be marked with metadata.sensitivity = "high" and require an approved security exception before enabled in non-private envs. - Terraform state for flag modules is stored in the same backend as infra state but with a separate key prefix and read ACL restricted to infra service accounts only.
appendix_examples_and_snippets:
Conflict detection Rego pseudo-rule: `deny[msg] { input.flag1.enabled == true; input.flag2.enabled == true; msg = sprintf("%v conflicts with %v", [input.flag1.name, input.flag2.name]) }`

Sample flags table (informal):
| flag_name | component | default | owner | sensitivity |
| serving_kernel_x_v2 | serving-runtime | false | serving-runtime | medium |
| kv_cache_prefetch_v2 | cache | false | storage-team | low |
| mixed_precision_global | runtime | true | serving-runtime | low |

next_steps: - Pilot with two low-risk flags (kv_cache_prefetch_v2, serving_kernel_x_v2) in staging within 2 sprints.\n- Add OPA policies to the central CI pipeline and enforce on all infra repos.\n- Schedule a runbook game-day with SRE and serving-runtime to exercise automated rollback.
notes: This pattern intentionally prioritizes auditability and small-step rollouts over speed. For emergency patches we keep an approved escape hatch documented in the runbook_snippets. Please send implementation questions to the owners listed above.
